253.title: Let nothing disturb thee
253.hook: a short poem found in her breviary: all things pass, God does not change, God alone suffices
253.howItsDone: Many Catholics keep Teresa's Nada te turbe on a prayer card or say it in hard moments, and the Taizé community sings it as a short, repeated chant.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventh rooms, spiritual marriage at the center of the castle. Your line was martha and mary together. Did you stop for three breaths before a job? Today, our last day with Teresa, and nine short lines. Day two hundred fifty-three.

A note folded in a wallet. A line taped inside a cabinet. A verse on a sticky note on the bathroom mirror. Something short enough to read with a toothbrush in your mouth, and strong enough to get through a day. Teresa of Ávila had one too. Tradition says that after she died, her sisters found it tucked in her breviary, the prayer book she carried every day. Nine lines. People still copy them out. Today's word is its first line.
screen: `A SCRAP OF PAPER, KEPT CLOSE.` → `TUCKED IN HER PRAYER BOOK.` → `NINE LINES.`

segments.voice: In Teresa's Spanish, it begins: "Nada te turbe, nada te espante." Let nothing disturb you, nothing frighten you. The old English version begins, let nothing disturb thee. First, the worry. Teresa did not live a quiet life. She lived with lawsuits, sickness, travel on broken roads, officials who tried to shut down her convents. These lines aren't a greeting card. They read like what a hard-pressed woman told herself. Second, what passes. The next lines say: everything passes. God does not change. Your worry, your triumph, your bad week, the officials who hate you, all of it passes. Only one thing stays still. Third, patience. Then: patience obtains everything. Not quick results. Patience. The kind of steady waiting she learned over a lifetime of prayer. Fourth, enough. And the ending, the part people carve on walls and stitch on cushions: whoever has God lacks nothing. And the last three words in Spanish: "Sólo Dios basta." God alone is enough. Here's what that doesn't mean. It doesn't mean Teresa didn't need friends, food or sleep. She loved her friends fiercely and wrote to them constantly. It means that underneath everything, when all of it shakes, there is a floor. For Teresa, that floor had a name. A week ago we walked through her castle door. Tomorrow, her little friend, John of the Cross, whom she loved and teased.
screen: `WRITTEN FROM A HARD LIFE.` · `ALL THINGS PASS. GOD DOES NOT.` · `PATIENCE OBTAINS EVERYTHING.` · `WHOEVER HAS GOD LACKS NOTHING.` · then, large: `SÓLO DIOS BASTA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write it on a card. Find a scrap of paper, a sticky note, anything. Write the first line, let nothing disturb thee, or the last, God alone is enough. Then hold it and breathe. Think of one thing that's disturbing you right now. Read the line to it. If you pray, you can pray Teresa's lines as she did. If you don't, let the words steady you. Put the card where you'll see it tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
Breviary. The prayer book Teresa carried every day, where her sisters found her nine lines after she died, including: God alone is enough. Today's word.
Your line: god alone is enough. Today, when something shakes you, read your card before you react. Day two hundred fifty-three. Teresa's castle, done. Tomorrow, John of the Cross.

254.title: The small friar (1542–1591)
254.hook: barely five feet tall; Teresa joked he was half a friar
254.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint John of the Cross on his feast day, December 14; Carmelite friars and nuns especially read his poems and books, and many Catholics know him through his teaching on the dark night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's nine lines: breviary. Your line was god alone is enough. Where did you put your card? Today, a new part of the path, and the friend Teresa loved and teased. Day two hundred fifty-four.

Teresa of Ávila has spent years founding reformed convents of Carmelite nuns. Now she wants to do the same for the men, and start a house of friars living the old, strict, prayerful way. She has found exactly two volunteers. One is an older priest, a solid, respectable man. The other is a young priest in his twenties, thin, quiet, and very short. She's delighted with both. And, the story goes, she joked that she now had a friar and a half to begin with. Today's word is the half.
screen: `TERESA WANTS FRIARS TOO.` → `TWO VOLUNTEERS.` → `A FRIAR AND A HALF.`

segments.voice: The half was John of the Cross. For the next eighteen days, this part of our path follows him. First, the size. Accounts put him at a little under five feet tall. Small, thin, often ill. He'd go on to write poems and books on prayer that are still read. But on the day Teresa met him, what people saw first was how little he was. Second, the joke. Teresa teased the people she loved. The friar-and-a-half line is affectionate, not cruel. She also nicknamed him her little Seneca, after the Roman philosopher, a fond joke about how serious and wise he was. Third, what she really thought. In a letter, Teresa wrote that though he was small, she understood him to be great in the eyes of God. It's an old pattern in the Bible. When the prophet Samuel goes looking for Israel's next king, he's impressed by the eldest brother's looks and height. And God tells him not to look at height or appearance, because people look at the outside and God looks at the heart. The king turns out to be the youngest son, out in the field with the sheep. Fourth, what comes. This small man would be kidnapped by his own order, locked in a closet-sized cell, escape through a window, and write a poem about a dark night that people still read. He was named a saint and a Doctor of the Church. And it all began with a joke about his height.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice greatness in someone small. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind someone easy to overlook. A quiet coworker, a child, an old neighbor, the person who cleans your building. Picture their face. What do they carry that nobody sees? What do they do well? If you pray, you can hold them before God for a moment. If you don't, just let yourself see them the way someone who loves them would. The bell holds the time.
Little Seneca. Teresa's fond nickname for John of the Cross, a small, serious friar she also called great in the eyes of God. Today's word.
Your line: half a friar. Today, say one true, specific word of praise to someone people usually overlook. Day two hundred fifty-four.

255.title: A poor childhood
255.hook: his father died young, and as a boy he worked in a hospital for the poor in Medina del Campo
255.howItsDone: Catholics remember John of the Cross's early years of poverty and hospital work, and visiting the sick is one of the corporal works of mercy in Catholic teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, little Seneca, whom Teresa teased as half a friar. Your line was half a friar. Who did you notice that people overlook? Today, we go back to where John started, and it's not a pretty place. Day two hundred fifty-five.

A young man from a comfortable family falls in love with a poor girl who weaves silk for a living. His family says: marry her, and you're out. He marries her anyway. They're cut off. They have three sons. They're poor, but they're together. Then, when the youngest is still a toddler, the father gets sick and dies. The mother walks for miles with her small children to ask the rich relatives for help. They mostly turn her away. The toddler grows up to be John of the Cross. Today's word is where he began.
screen: `A MARRIAGE FOR LOVE.` → `CUT OFF BY THE FAMILY.` → `THE FATHER DIES YOUNG.`

segments.voice: First, hunger. John was born Juan de Yepes in 1542, in a small Castilian town called Fontiveros. His father, Gonzalo, died when John was very small. His mother, Catalina, kept the family alive by weaving, moving from town to town looking for work. It wasn't enough. One of John's brothers, Luis, died young, and some biographers think hunger was part of it. Second, the school for poor children. The family finally settled in Medina del Campo, a busy market town. John was taken into a school for poor and orphaned children, where he got food, clothes and some learning. They tried to apprentice him to a trade: carpenter, tailor, woodcarver, painter. None of them stuck. Third, the hospital. As a teenager he went to work in a hospital for the poor, a place for people with contagious diseases. He washed patients, fed them, cleaned up after them, and went out begging in the streets to pay for their care. People who knew him then remembered how gentle he was with the sick. Fourth, the choice. The hospital's director saw something in him and paid for him to study with the Jesuits. He offered John a secure future: become a priest and stay on as the hospital's chaplain. For a poor boy, that was everything. John said no, and quietly joined the Carmelites at twenty-one. The man who later wrote about nights and nothingness wasn't theorizing. He knew poverty, hunger and sickrooms first.
screen: `A HUNGRY CHILDHOOD.` · `A SCHOOL FOR POOR CHILDREN.` · `WASHING THE SICK AS A TEENAGER.` · `HE TURNS DOWN A SAFE FUTURE.` · then, large: `HE KNEW POVERTY FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help one person who is unwell. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind someone you know who's sick right now, in body or in spirit. A friend in the hospital, a parent getting frail, a coworker who's been quietly struggling. Hold them in mind. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, send them good attention. Then decide on one small, concrete thing you'll do for them today: a text, a meal, a visit, a ride. The bell holds the time.
Hunger. What marked John of the Cross's childhood: a father's early death, a mother who wove for pennies, and a brother hunger may have taken too. Today's word.
Your line: he knew poverty first. Today, do the one small thing you decided for someone who is unwell, and do it before evening. Day two hundred fifty-five.

256.title: Meeting Teresa (1567)
256.hook: he joins her reform of the Carmelites: barefoot, poor, prayerful
256.howItsDone: The Discalced Carmelites, friars and nuns, still live Teresa and John's reform today, with hours of daily silent prayer, and many wear sandals as part of their habit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hunger, a hospital, and a safe future turned down. Your line was he knew poverty first. Did you do the small thing for someone unwell? Today, the young friar meets the woman who'll change his life. Day two hundred fifty-six.

Medina del Campo, 1567. John is twenty-five, newly ordained, and restless. He's a Carmelite, but he wants more silence and more prayer than his house gives him. He's quietly decided to leave and join the Carthusians, monks known for silence and solitude. Then someone tells a visiting nun about him. She's older, well known, and in town to open a new convent. She asks to meet him. They talk. And by the end of the conversation, he isn't going anywhere. Today's word is what she talked him into.
screen: `A RESTLESS YOUNG PRIEST.` → `ABOUT TO LEAVE FOR MORE SILENCE.` → `ONE CONVERSATION WITH TERESA.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Discalced comes from the Latin for unshod, without shoes. Teresa's reformed Carmelites were called the Discalced, the barefoot ones. In practice they usually wore simple rope sandals, not bare feet on Spanish stone. But the name stuck, and it said what they were about: poverty, simplicity, a life stripped down for prayer. Second, the pitch. Teresa told John he didn't need to leave the Carmelites to find silence. He could help her bring it back to them. She was already reforming convents of nuns. Now she wanted a house of friars living the same way: poor, enclosed, praying for hours a day. He agreed, on one condition: that she not make him wait too long. Third, the farmhouse. In 1568 he moved into the first house of Discalced friars, in a tiny hamlet called Duruelo. It was a half-ruined farmhouse. The choir for prayer was up in the loft, so low at the sides that the friars had to stoop. Teresa visited and said later it moved her deeply. That's when he took a new name, John of the Cross. Fourth, the shoes. Why shoes? At the burning bush, God tells Moses, in the Douay-Rheims: "put off the shoes from thy feet: for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." Taking off shoes is an old sign: you're somewhere holy, and you're not in charge here. The Discalced wanted to live their whole life that way. Not everyone welcomed the reform, though. Tomorrow we'll see how some of John's own brothers answered it.
screen: `DISCALCED: WITHOUT SHOES.` · `DON'T LEAVE. HELP ME REFORM.` · `A FARMHOUSE IN DURUELO.` · `SHOES OFF ON HOLY GROUND.` · then, large: `PUT OFF THE SHOES FROM THY FEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take off your shoes for prayer. If you're wearing shoes, slip them off, and feel the floor under your feet. If you're driving or can't, just picture it. Sit, and let your feet rest flat. Notice the ground holding you up. If you pray, you can treat this little spot as holy ground for two minutes, and simply be present to God there. If you don't, let the bare feet remind you to slow down and be where you are. The bell holds the time.
Discalced. From the Latin for unshod: Teresa and John's reformed Carmelites, living poor, simple and prayerful, often in rope sandals. Today's word.
Your line: the barefoot friars. Today, find one thing you could strip down, a routine, a closet, a calendar, and take one thing out of it. Day two hundred fifty-six.

257.title: The Toledo cell (1577)
257.hook: his own order kidnaps him and locks him in a tiny cell for nine months
257.howItsDone: Catholics count visiting the imprisoned among the corporal works of mercy, and many parishes run prison ministries; pilgrims to Toledo can visit the site associated with John's imprisonment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Discalced, Teresa's barefoot friars, and a farmhouse at Duruelo. Your line was the barefoot friars. What did you strip down? Today, the reform costs John almost everything. Day two hundred fifty-seven.

Ávila, a winter night in December 1577. John is living in a small house beside a convent of nuns, where he serves as their confessor. There's a crash at the door. Men burst in, some of them friars of his own order, some armed. They seize him, take his papers, and lead him away blindfolded. He's taken to Toledo, to their priory above the river. There they put him in a room. Then they lock the door. He'll be in that room for nine months, and almost nobody knows where he is. Today's word is that room.
screen: `A WINTER NIGHT IN ÁVILA.` → `SEIZED BY HIS OWN BROTHERS.` → `TAKEN TO TOLEDO.`

segments.voice: First, why. This wasn't a random crime. It came out of a bitter fight inside the Carmelite order. The older branch, often called the Calced, the ones who wore shoes, saw Teresa's reform as a split, and as disobedience to their superiors. The Discalced saw it as a return to the order's first ideals. Church officials gave conflicting orders, and both sides believed they were in the right. John was caught in the middle. It's worth saying: both branches are still part of the Catholic Church today, and they live in peace. Second, the cell. The room was a closet, roughly six feet by ten, once used as a storeroom off a guest room. There was no window, only a narrow slit high in the wall. To read his prayer book, John had to stand on a bench at midday and catch the thin light. In winter it froze. In summer it baked. Third, the treatment. He was fed bread and water, sometimes scraps of sardine. He wore the same habit for months, and lice crawled through it. At first he was brought to the dining hall and beaten while the friars ate, and told that the reform was finished and that Teresa had given up on him. Fourth, what he did. He was ordered to renounce the reform. He refused. And there, in the dark, sick and alone, he began to do something no one expected. We'll hear it tomorrow. For now, Jesus's words about the last judgment: "I was in prison, and you came to me."
screen: `A FIGHT INSIDE ONE ORDER.` · `A CLOSET SIX FEET BY TEN.` · `BREAD, WATER, BEATINGS, LICE.` · `ORDERED TO RENOUNCE. HE REFUSED.` · then, large: `I WAS IN PRISON, AND YOU CAME TO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for anyone imprisoned. Settle and breathe. Think of people locked away right now: in prisons and jails, in detention, held hostage, or shut in by illness, fear or a hard home. You don't have to know their names. If you know one, hold that one. If you pray, you can ask God to be with them in their dark room. If you don't, simply hold them in mind for two minutes, and remember they're there. The bell holds the time.
Toledo. The city where John was imprisoned nine months in a closet-sized room of the Carmelite priory, from December 1577. Today's word.
Your line: the dark room. Today, when you feel stuck somewhere small, a car, a meeting, a mood, remember the people who can't leave theirs. Day two hundred fifty-seven.

258.title: Poems in the dark
258.hook: in prison he composes his great love poem in his head
258.howItsDone: Carmelites and many other Catholics read and pray John's poems, especially the Spiritual Canticle, and memorizing psalms and short scripture verses remains a common Catholic devotional habit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Toledo: a closet, a slit of light, nine months. Your line was the dark room. Who did you hold in mind that can't leave theirs? Today, what John did in there. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

Lock a person in a closet for months, no phone, no books, no paper, and what does the mind do? It could replay every wrong ever done to it. It could plan revenge, or despair, or both. John of the Cross, cold and sick in his cell in Toledo, did something else. He started making poems. Not angry poems. Love poems. He had nothing to write with, so he composed them in his head, line by line, and kept them there, memorized, in the dark. Poems still read today began that way. Today's word is that work.
screen: `NO PHONE, NO BOOKS, NO PAPER.` → `NOT REVENGE. LOVE POEMS.` → `MEMORIZED IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: First, the Canticle. One poem he began there is known as the Spiritual Canticle. It's a love song, modeled on the Song of Songs in the Bible. A bride searches everywhere for her beloved, who has slipped away. For John, the bride is the soul and the beloved is God. He made the first part of it in that cell, keeping the stanzas in memory. Second, the kind jailer. After some months, the story goes, a new, younger friar was put in charge of him. He was gentler, let John out to empty his bucket, and gave him a pen and a little paper. That's how some of the poems survived. Third, the spring. One of the poems from the cell has a refrain that keeps coming back, in John's Spanish: "Que bien sé yo la fonte que mana y corre, aunque es de noche." How well I know the spring that rushes and flows, although it is night. Remember where he made it. No light. No news. And he says: I know where the water is. Even now. Even at night. Fourth, the psalms. He wasn't making it all up from nothing. For years he had prayed the psalms day after day, in the Church's daily prayer. When everything else was taken away, what was inside his memory was still his. The Bible's love poetry and the psalms' cries were the raw material. In the Douay-Rheims: "For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me." What you've memorized can't be confiscated.
screen: `A LOVE SONG FOR THE SOUL.` · `A KIND JAILER, A LITTLE PAPER.` · `I KNOW THE SPRING, THOUGH IT IS NIGHT.` · `WHAT YOU KNOW BY HEART STAYS.` · then, large: `AUNQUE ES DE NOCHE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: memorize one line of a psalm. Try this one: though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me. Say it once slowly. Then again, with your eyes closed. Then once more, only in your head. If you pray, let it be a prayer. If you don't, let it be something to carry that no one can take. By the bell, it's yours. The bell holds the time.

Your line: songs in prison. Today, say your psalm line from memory at least three times: waking, midday, and before sleep. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

259.title: The escape (1578)
259.hook: a rope of torn blankets, a drop over the wall, and a convent of nuns hides him
259.howItsDone: Catholics tell the story of John's escape as part of his life, and the Discalced Carmelite nuns of Toledo, who hid him, are remembered in that story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Spiritual Canticle: a love song kept in memory, and a spring that flows though it is night. Your line was songs in prison. Did your psalm line stay with you? Today, John goes out the window. Day two hundred fifty-nine.

August 1578, Toledo, a hot summer night. John has been locked in his cell for almost nine months. He's weak and thin. But he's been paying attention. On the short trips to empty his bucket he's studied the hallway and a window that looks out over the city wall and the river. He's loosened the screws on his door lock, a little at a time. He's torn his two blankets into strips and knotted them into a rope. Tonight the friars are asleep. He pushes the door. It opens.

segments.voice: First, the drop. He creeps past sleeping friars to the window, ties his blanket rope to something solid, and climbs out over a sheer drop above the river. The rope is too short. At the end of it he lets go, and falls. He lands on the edge of a wall, hurt but alive, and jumps down into a walled courtyard he doesn't recognize. Trapped again, it seems, until he finds a way to climb out into the street. Second, the dawn. Barefoot, filthy, in a ragged habit, he waits in the dark streets of Toledo until morning. Then he makes his way to the one place he knows will take him: the convent of Discalced Carmelite nuns, Teresa's sisters. Third, the nuns. The prioress sees at once what's happening. Friars will soon be searching the city. So she brings him inside the enclosure, where outsiders can't follow, with a perfectly true excuse: a sick sister needs a confessor. He hides there for hours. Feeble as he is, he recites the poems he made in the dark, and the nuns write them down. Some of his poetry may have survived because of that afternoon. Fourth, the week. Look back at these seven days: Teresa's nine lines, God alone is enough. A small friar, hunger, a meeting that kept him in the order. A dark room in Toledo, poems made in memory, and tonight a rope of blankets. It's the middle of John's story, and the hinge. What he learned in that room, he'll spend the rest of his life writing down. Tomorrow, the poem behind a phrase people still use: the dark night.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave something that holds you. Settle and breathe. Think of one small thing that keeps you locked in. A habit, a resentment, an app, a story about yourself that isn't true anymore. Picture it as a locked room, and yourself loosening the screws, one at a time. What's one screw you could loosen today? If you pray, you can ask God for courage to climb out. If you don't, just name the first step. The bell holds the time.
